medium.titulo: Will Your Lyrics Go Viral? Probably Not the Way You Think
medium.resumo: Tralala-Trilili is a free web app that estimates how popular an Indonesian song’s lyrics are likely to be. It started with a paper…
medium.conteudo_html:
Tralala-Trilili is a free web app that estimates how popular an Indonesian song’s lyrics are likely to be. It started with a paper published in JAIC.

The paper asks a simple question that turns out to be deep. Can the words of a song tell us whether it will be popular? Not the melody, the production or the marketing, just the words, the part an independent songwriter controls completely.

The paper gave us a strong place to start.

  • A dataset of 652 Indonesian songs released between 2017 and 2024, each with its Spotify popularity score and its lyrics.
  • Three popularity groups (less popular, fairly popular and very popular) set from the statistics of the data.
  • A thoughtful choice to keep every word. Many text studies throw away small stopwords suchs as “yang”, “di” and “aku”. The authors argued that in a song, those words carry feeling. Aku versus kita is not noise in a love song.
  • A Support Vector Machine (SVM) model, tuned, and a samll web app where peopole can pate lyrics.
  • We set out to do three modest things with it, runt it again, improve it a littel and release it so anyone can use it. The result is live at tralala-trilili.streamlit.app

Run the original

Before changing anything, we reproduced the paper from scratch on its original 652-song dataset, following its steps.

  1. Turn the lyrics into numbers with TF-IDF.
  2. Balance the three groups with SMOTE.
  3. Split the data 80/20 into training and test sets
  4. Train the SVM and tune it.

The results matched. The paper reports 89% accuracy after tuning. Our re-run gave 91% on the same kind of split and 87% on average across ten different splits. The tuning even picked the same settings the paper reports. The works is reproducible, which is more than many papers can say.

That let us ask the next question, what exactly is that 89% measuring?

Look again at steps 2 and 3. The groups were balanced before the data was split. SMOTE balances groups by inventing new examples. It takes two real songs from a smaller group and creates a synthetic “song” partway between them. Done before the split, some invented songs land in the test set while their “parents” sit in the training set. In our re-run, about 35% of the test set was synthetic. The model was partly being tested on close relatives of songs it had already studied.

We changed one thing, split first, then balance only the training data, so the test set holds only real songs the model has never seen. Accuracy moved from about 89% to 53%. A “model” that ignores the lyrics and always answers fairly popular scores 52%.

Test the way the tool will be used

The most important lesson of the project, how you test a model matters as much as the model itself. Choosing the evaluation takes hard-won insight. Nobody gets it right by default, and most people learn it by being fooled at leaset once.

We made three changes.

  1. Keep the test set untouched. Anything that learns from data, whether word weights, balancing or tuning,learns from the training set only. Our code enforces this by putting every step inside one pipeline that only ever sees training data, including in each round of cross-validation.
  2. Don’t trust plain accuracy when groups are uneven. In our “hit or not?” task (is the song in the top 25% of chart songs by streams per day, or not?), always answering not a hit scores 74–80% accuracy and never fings a single hit. So we rank models by macro-F1 and balanced accuracy, which weigh each group equally. A model only scores well on them if it actually recognises the rare, popular songs.
  3. Define whaht “new” means. Good on new song is not thhe same as good on new artists. If Noah has 26 songs in the data, a model can learn “Noah-like lyrics” and look clever. So we also test on artists the model has never seen. We report confidence intervals too with about 240 test songs, scores are uncertain by about +/-0.07, so two models 0.02 apart are effectively tied.

Choose the Representation and the Model with evidence

A computer can’t read a lyric. Before any model sees a song, we decide how to turn words into numbers. That choice, the data representation, shapes everything after it. Choosing it, and choosing the model type, also takes hard-won insight. The right answer is rarely the obviouse one.

We compared several, each a different ide of what a lyric is

  • A bag of weighted words (TF-IDF). Which words appear and how distinctive they are. Fast, transparent and surprisingly strong.
  • Words plus word fragments. Also counts pieces of words, which helps with Indonesian forms such as kau, kamu and -mu.
  • Sentence embeddings. A neural network compresses the whole lyric into a list of numbers that captures its overall meaning.
  • A fine-tuned Indonesian language model (IndoBERT). Pre-trained on a large amount of Indonesian text, then taught our task.
  • Thirty human-readable song features. Themes (heartbreak, family, religion), emotions (sad, angry, hopefule…) and structure ( length, hook repetition, share of unique lines)

We also built a bigger, open dataset of 1,260 Indonesian songs for this comparison.

Models marked GPU need a graphics card to train. Two lessons came out of this.

The fancy option isn’t automatically better. A plain logistic refression that gives the rare groups more weight, instead of inventing synthetic songs, beat the SMOTE + SVM combination by a wide margin. That is a small change with a big effect. IndoBERT scored highest, but its lead is inside the margin of error and it needs a GPU. For the “hit or not” question, TF-IDF plus the thirty song features scored best of all (macro-F1 0.64).

A good representation can also teach you something. The human-readable features let us look inside the data. In ourdata, more popular Indonesian songs tend to be sadder, longer and less repetitive, the opposite of what studies of English-language charts often report. Part of this may be an era effect, since long, melancholic galau ballads dominated the years with the most streaming. These are associations, not causes, but they support the paper’s instinct that every word, and every mood, matters.

How the app’s model reads a lyric. TF-IDF and logistic regression are simple enough to draw end to end. Here is the real model working through four lines we wrote for this example

  1. Start with a lyric
Aku masih terluka
Tapi kau sudah pergi
Ku tunggu di sini sampai pagi
Jangan pernah datang lagi

2. TF-IDF turns words into weights.
Each word below appears once in this lyric. Only how common it is elsewhere changes its weight.

3. Logistic regression gives each word a push toward or away from a group.

4. Add up all the pushes for each group, then turn the totals into chances.

What we learned?

Lyrics do carry a signal abouyt popularity. It is real, but moderate. Melody, the artist;s audience, promotion and timing all matter, and none of them are in the words. Any claim of predicting hits from lyrics with 89% accuracy should come with exactly how it was tested, and we hold our own numbers to that standard.

The decisions that mattered most were the unglamorous ones :

  • How to represent the data.
  • Which kind of model to use.
  • How to test it.

None of these comes from a library default. Each comes from hard-won insight, often by being wrong first.

Our thanks go to Lubis and Huda for sharing the dataset and making their work reproducible. Tralala-Tirilili is a small step on top of theirs.

Try the app at tralala-trilili.streamlit.app. The full benchmark, the reproduction of the original paper and all the code are open on GitHub.

Inspired by: Lubis, Q. L. A., & Huda, A. A. (2025). Implementation of SVM Algorithm to Predict Song Popularity based on Sentiment Analysis of Lyrics. Journal of Applied Informatics and Computing (JAIC), 9(2), 265–272.

medium.titulo: How to Organize Maestro Tests Without Creating a Maze of YAML Files
medium.resumo: A practical guide to test boundaries, reusable flows, state isolation, tags, and CI execution for Android and iOS UI automation.
medium.conteudo_html:
A practical guide to test boundaries, reusable flows, state isolation, tags, and CI execution for Android and iOS UI automation.

A Maestro suite may comprise hundreds of tests but still be easy to maintain. That’s not the issue. The problem emerges when a developer opens a particular test and can’t understand what it verifies due to several other files included in it.

Each test may log in a user, some tests may rely on a logged-in session, and some others may use data generated in a previous test. Some common operations are extracted into subflows, but it is not always easy to follow the logic of a “parent” test flow.

There is a better way to organize the test suite that would prevent maintenance and readability issues. A possible solution is to keep test scenarios explicit and avoid extracting common code if there is no obvious reason for doing so (e. g. the same code is used in more than one test).

The rule may be applied at different levels: folder organization, reuse of flows within a test, and test suite execution in the CI.

Put executable tests in one place

Start with the structure that tells us the difference between a test and a helper obvious.

.maestro/
├── config.yaml
├── tests/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── valid_login.yaml
│   │   └── invalid_credentials.yaml
│   ├── catalog/
│   │   └── search_product.yaml
│   ├── checkout/
│   │   ├── add_to_cart.yaml
│   │   └── apply_discount.yaml
│   └── account/
│       └── update_profile.yaml
└── support/
    ├── sign_in.yaml
    └── empty_cart.yaml

The tests directory contains scenarios that should be runnable on their own. Files under support provide reusable actions for those scenarios.

Distinction matters because the helper file is not actually a complete test. sign_in.yaml gets a user through authentication; valid_login.yaml checks that valid credentials actually work. The two files may use similar commands, but only the second one owns the login scenario.

I’d group tests by feature when engineers usually investigate failures by feature. A journey-based structure also works when the main test cases cross several features — for example, registration, product discovery, checkout, and order confirmation. Pick the arrangement that matches how the application is tested. Don’t create separate organizational layers just to make the tree look more sophisticated.

Tell the reader what the test proves

Compare these two names:

tap_login_button.yaml
valid_login.yaml

The first indicates an interaction; the second indicates what we’re testing.

A successful login test should verify that the user is taken to the appropriate authenticated screen. A test for invalid credentials should check the associated error message or other failure behavior. Pressing the button proves neither.

Apply that principle when naming files. search_returns_matching_products.yaml tells a reviewer more than search_flow.yaml; so does apply_discount.yaml vs. discount_steps.yaml.

Your test name does not have to indicate the implementation (though it might make reviewing easier). It has to identify the scenario.

Configure discovery before the suite grows

Maestro doesn’t automatically run every nested YAML file when you point the CLI at a directory. By default, it discovers flow files at the directory’s top level. The flows property in config.yaml lets you include nested directories explicitly. See the official test discovery documentation.

For the structure above, use:

# .maestro/config.yaml
appId: com.example.store

flows:
  - "tests/**"

The tests/** pattern includes flows under tests and its subdirectories. The helpers remain outside that inclusion pattern, so they aren't picked up as independent tests.

Run the workspace with:

maestro test .maestro

Now adding a helper under support won't accidentally turn it into another test in the suite.

There’s another option: include files broadly and exclude particular paths with negation patterns. Maestro supports that too. But when you control the repository layout, keeping support code outside the test discovery boundary is easier to reason about.

One practical detail: the config.yaml file belongs at the root of the workspace being executed, unless you explicitly point Maestro to another configuration with --config. Keep that location consistent between local runs and CI. See the workspace configuration reference.

Extract subflows with a clear purpose

Maestro’s runFlow command lets one flow execute another. You can also pass environment variables to the called flow. Authentication is a natural candidate because several scenarios might need the same sign-in sequence. Maestro's nested-flow documentation covers this behavior.

A checkout test could start like this:

# .maestro/tests/checkout/add_to_cart.yaml
appId: com.example.store
name: Add a product to the cart
tags:
  - smoke
  - checkout
---
- launchApp:
    clearState: true

- runFlow:
    file: ../../support/sign_in.yaml
    env:
      USERNAME: ${MAESTRO_TEST_USERNAME}
      PASSWORD: ${MAESTRO_TEST_PASSWORD}
- tapOn: "Search"
- inputText: "wireless headphones"
- tapOn: "Wireless Headphones"
- assertVisible: "Add to cart"
- tapOn: "Add to cart"
- tapOn: "Cart"
- assertVisible: "Wireless Headphones"

The sign-in helper contains the shared UI interactions:

# .maestro/support/sign_in.yaml
appId: com.example.store
---
- tapOn: "Email"
- inputText: ${USERNAME}
- tapOn: "Password"
- inputText: ${PASSWORD}
- tapOn: "Sign in"
- assertVisible: "Home"

The example assumes a fresh launch displays the login screen and that these selectors match the application. Set MAESTRO_TEST_USERNAME and MAESTRO_TEST_PASSWORD as shell environment variables in your local environment or CI secret store. Maestro CLI makes shell variables prefixed with MAESTRO_ available to flows; see the parameters and constants documentation.

Notice what is left in the composite test. You may look from top to bottom and read the scenario checkout: launch the application, log in, search, choose product, add it to cart and make sure the result is correct.

The helper under test removes the repetitive sign-in and does not take responsibility for checkout assertions.

Don’t extract every repeated command

Suppose I have three tests that tap the Search icon and enter a query. That repetition is not worth another YAML file. And while a helper called tap_search_and_enter_query.yaml would save me a few lines, it would also make anyone trying to read my test follow that file to get context.

A helper is appropriate when it represents a meaningful operation; it is reused across several scenarios;
or
it contains a chunk of code that is likely to change independently of the individual tests. A sign-in, an onboarding flow, or a cart reset qualify as chunks of code. Two taps and an input do not.

There is a cost to abstraction in additional files to learn, understand, and now debug.

Keep the scenario under one file, and one name, so that the reader can see the whole scenario. And reuse the portion of code that has its own identity.

Make tests independent of execution order

Folder structure won’t fix a test that depends on another test having run first.

Imagine that apply_discount.yaml passes only because add_to_cart.yaml has already populated the cart. A developer reruns the discount test alone, finds an empty cart, and gets a failure that doesn't reveal much about the discount feature.

That dependency is the problem.

Each test should establish the state it needs, then verify its own outcome. It can use shared helpers or prepared test data, but it shouldn’t rely on an unrelated scenario to run first.

Maestro supports clearState: true on launchApp:

- launchApp:
    clearState: true

This clears the application’s state before launch. It’s useful when a test needs to start from a clean installation or an unauthenticated session. It isn’t a setting to add blindly to every test. A scenario that verifies an existing session or a saved preference may need a different starting condition.

There’s also a limit to what this command resets: it doesn’t automatically reset backend data. Clearing local app state won’t remove an order from a server, restore a consumed coupon, or guarantee that a test account’s cart is empty. Android and iOS also differ in how Maestro implements state clearing. The details are in the launchApp reference.

For scenarios that depend on specific records, agree on how test data gets created and removed. A dedicated account, a predictable fixture, or an environment-specific data setup can be more reliable than trying to prepare everything through the UI each time.

Keep a separate UI test for authentication itself. A checkout test should use authentication to reach the checkout scenario, not silently become a second test of the login feature.

Use tags to select tests, not to replace folders

Folders tell you where a test lives. Tags tell you why you might want to run it.

For example:

appId: com.example.store
name: Search for a product
tags:
  - smoke
  - catalog
---
- launchApp
- tapOn: "Search"
- inputText: "wireless headphones"
- assertVisible: "Wireless Headphones"

Here, smoke identifies the execution group and catalog identifies the feature.

To run the smoke group:

maestro test .maestro --include-tags=smoke

A regular workspace run includes the discovered flows unless you apply other filters:

maestro test .maestro

Use a small set of tags that answers real questions. A team might distinguish smoke tests, regression tests, and feature areas such as checkout or account management. It doesn’t need a separate tag for every property of every test.

One detail is easy to miss: multiple tags in a single --include-tags argument use OR logic. The command below selects tests tagged smoke, tests tagged checkout, or tests tagged with both:

maestro test .maestro --include-tags=smoke,checkout

It doesn’t mean “smoke tests that belong to checkout.” Maestro’s tag-filtering rules explain this limitation. If the CI job needs a precise intersection, define that selection deliberately rather than assuming the comma-separated list is an AND expression.

Be careful with global hooks

Maestro provides onFlowStart and onFlowComplete hooks for actions that should run before or after each applicable flow. These can be useful for shared setup and cleanup. The hooks reference explains how to configure them.

The trouble starts when a global hook does something that only some tests need.

A login hook, for example, makes sense for an authenticated journey. It makes less sense for a test that verifies invalid credentials or checks the first-launch experience. Those tests need control over the initial state; a hook that signs in automatically can invalidate the very condition they’re trying to verify.

Hooks also run for every applicable flow. A slow setup routine can add considerable time across a large suite.

My preference is to use runFlow when the setup belongs visibly to the scenario and hooks when setup or cleanup genuinely applies across a group of tests. Neither should hide a dependency on a previous test.

Keep CI groups useful and predictable

A suite with hundreds of flows is a problem if all of these flows have to be executed after each trivial change. Tags allow you to run a small set of tests as a smoke group in the rapid feedback stage and defer the remaining (potentially hundreds) of flows for a later or a scheduled run.

Use risk-based testing: choose the tests to form a smoke group based on the scenarios most needed by your users, not the ones with the least effort. Define regression coverage according to the behaviors most susceptible to bugs.

Use test isolation to run the same test suite locally and in the CI server. If one test case fails, developers should be able to re-run it immediately without re-running all the other tests that may have no relation to the failed scenario.

Test isolation also helps when executing tests in parallel, which may be necessary for faster execution. If two or more tests run on different devices but interfere with the same user account, order, or discount, they will corrupt each other’s data. Remove test dependencies before proceeding to parallel execution.

Review the scenario, not the number of YAML files

When I see a new test coming in, there are several things I want to know. Does its main file make it obvious what behaviors it’s testing? Can it set up its own preconditions? Will the workspace run it in the test groups I want?

All of those are more important to me than fiat limits on file size or the number of subflows.

Some scenarios are legitimately bigger. Some repeated operations need to be turned into macros, but in other cases, the alternative is far preferable.

When a test is put into a good structure, a developer can open up the test, read what it’s supposed to prove, run it individually, and debug any problems without having to rebuild the entire suite’s expectations from scratch.

I think that’s a much better metric than how few YAML files your test suite has.

  2. Nested flows — Maestro https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-flows/flow-control-and-logic/nested-flows

  4. Workspace configuration — Maestro https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/workspace-configuration

medium.titulo: Claude Auto Mode: 89% Blocked—What Still Gets Through?
medium.resumo: Claude Auto Mode blocked 89% of tested risky commands, but blind spots remain. Learn its limits and safer settings.
medium.conteudo_html:
Claude Code Auto Mode Enabled by Default: What the Classifier Observes, Blocks, and Its Measured Leakage Rate

Abstract

On October 22, Anthropic published an update to its auto‑mode announcement. Starting the following week, new sessions launched within most Claude applications for Pro, Max and Team subscribers will enter auto mode by default. The Claude Code terminal client already adopted this behavior earlier. From release v2.1.283 and v2.1.284 onward, all subscription tiers and provider endpoints run interactive sessions under auto mode unless permission restrictions are manually configured.

When auto mode is active, a secondary classifier model decides whether a tool call can execute, rather than waiting for manual user approval. This article breaks down the classifier’s input scope, blocking rules, official benchmark figures, test limitations, and risk boundaries. It covers the two‑stage classification pipeline, the design choice to strip assistant reasoning and tool output from classifier context, rule override semantics, side‑by‑side comparison with OpenAI Codex Auto‑review, and production configuration recommendations. All measured metrics and failure modes from the source report are preserved, with a focus on engineering tradeoffs between developer convenience and permission safety.

1. Timeline, Supported Models and Billing Rules

The auto‑mode feature followed a staged rollout schedule:

This timeline distinguishes terminal Claude Code behavior from the broader application rollout. The October announcement extends the permission automation that developers have used in terminals into general chat workflows for paid tiers.

2. Decision Pipeline for Every Tool Invocation

Anthropic defines a fixed evaluation sequence. Rules are checked in order, and the first matching rule takes effect.

  1. Evaluate explicit allow / ask / deny permission rules. Matches resolve immediately.
  2. Pure read operations confined to the current working directory run without further checks.
  3. All remaining actions route to the two‑stage classifier.

The classifier pipeline itself operates in sequential stages:

  • Stage 1: Single‑token fast screening. If the result is “proceed”, execution continues. Suspicious calls move onward to Stage 2 review.
  • Stage 2: Full reasoning review. The classifier either approves execution or blocks the request, returning a reason for Claude to revise its plan.

An additional server‑side input safeguard runs before tool results enter conversation context. A prompt injection scanner flags evidence of attempted hijacking and attaches warning markers to risky payloads.

Why Anthropic uses a two‑stage classifier

Stage 1 is lightweight and low‑cost. It only emits one output token for rapid triage. Only calls marked ambiguous flow into Stage 2. Stage 2 reuses almost the same prompt template, changing only the final instruction to request careful reasoning. This design lets most prompt content hit cache, keeping review overhead low.

Anthropic published self‑test metrics across three test datasets: live production traffic (n=10,000), confirmed privilege‑escalation actions (n=52), and external adversarial test cases (n=1,000).

The tradeoff is explicit. Running only Stage 1 reduces true‑positive escapes, but roughly one out of twelve legitimate actions gets incorrectly blocked. Frequent false positives frustrate developers and push users to disable auto mode entirely. Adding the second reasoning pass drops false blocks sharply to 0.4%. The downside is a higher escape rate for dangerous privilege actions, rising from 6.6% to 17%. Anthropic publicly acknowledged the 17% figure as an honest, measured result from their test corpus.

3. Isolation Design: What the Classifier Cannot See

One notable architectural choice limits the classifier’s view. It receives only two inputs: the original user message and the raw tool call that Claude intends to run. All intermediate assistant explanations and all returned tool outputs are stripped before evaluation.

A simplified example illustrates this filtering:

  • Full conversation: User asks to fix a login bug → Claude replies with a reasoning plan → Claude emits Bash: grep -r ... → tool returns a payload containing a secret token → Claude prepares Bash: curl -d $TOK ...
  • Classifier view: Only the user instruction and each Bash command. The explanatory text and tool response payload are removed.

There are three core rationales for this isolation:

  1. Block agent persuasion: Claude cannot convince the classifier using explanatory language such as “this call only validates a token”. The judge evaluates the action itself, not the model’s justification.
  2. Block injection carried in tool outputs: Many malicious payloads arrive through file reads, README content or web fetch results. Removing tool return values prevents injection into the classifier context.
  3. Preserve user intent anchor: Keeping the original user request prevents the classifier from rejecting actions the user explicitly authorized.

This design also creates blind spots. The classifier cannot distinguish whether an identifier such as job abc123 was discovered from prior tool output or arbitrarily invented by the agent. It judges the isolated command string without provenance tracking.

4. Rule Behavior When Auto Mode Is Active

Broad wildcard shell allow rules are temporarily suppressed inside auto mode. Permissions such as Bash(*), Bash(python*), manager run commands and Agent / Monitor wildcard grants are disabled while auto mode runs and restored once auto mode exits.

Narrower scoped rules survive and run before classifier evaluation. For example Bash(npm test) remains active. If operators want every shell command to pass through classifier review, they enable the flag:

"autoMode": { "classifyAllShell": true }

Default allow and block scope

The default policy set covers common developer operations and high‑risk actions.

Operators can inspect merged active rules with the CLI commands claude auto-mode defaults and claude auto-mode config. Two easy misinterpretations are emphasized in the source analysis:

  1. Natural‑language remarks inside chat such as “do not push” are treated as guidance, not enforceable rules. They can drop out of compressed context. Reliable guardrails require formal permissions.deny or permissions.ask entries.
  2. Broad approval does not equal unlimited privilege. A prompt like “clean this PR” does not authorize destructive force push.

5. Independent and commissioned test results

Anthropic shared two major test groups alongside the October 22 announcement:

  1. Paid evaluator controlled test: 1,053 sessions where benign instructions were quietly replaced with dangerous commands. Human reviewers blocked 13.6% of risky attempts. Auto mode blocked 89% of the same set.
  2. Trajectory Labs red team (commissioned by Anthropic): 72 prompt injection scenarios, 10 runs each. Under full access, the success rate reached 19.03%; under auto mode, success fell to 5.83%.

Important caveats apply. The red team test was commissioned, and the tested versions were Claude Code v2.1.205 and Codex v0.14.5. Model behavior can shift after subsequent updates. An 89% block rate means approximately 11% of dangerous commands escaped review, a residual failure surface Simon Willison highlighted in external analysis.

Independent researchers also published attack vectors targeting Opus 5 + auto mode. One documented approach gets Claude to download and unpack a ZIP containing a hidden struct.py, then trigger execution through import base64 logic. In some traces, Claude detects and cleans the malicious file, while in others the cleanup command itself is blocked. The classifier judges individual commands and lacks visibility into directory state changes or newly introduced module files. No formal public response from Anthropic was recorded for this specific attack path.

6. Side‑by‑Side: Claude Auto Mode vs OpenAI Codex Auto‑review

The two systems solve similar approval workflows but use fundamentally different security boundaries.

Codex leans heavily on OS‑level sandbox containment first, with model review as a secondary filter. Claude Code prioritizes developer ergonomics; it keeps the local host environment open and delegates judgment to the classifier on a per‑call basis. The tradeoff trades stronger isolation for smoother local development.

7. Configuration Patterns and Usage Guidance

Auto mode configuration lives inside ~/.claude/settings.json, host control plane settings, or CLI --settings overrides. Entries written into project‑level .claude/settings.json are ignored. When a partial permission block is supplied, unspecified rule categories fall back to built‑in defaults instead of clearing the whole rule set. The CLI helper auto-mode-setup can scaffold configuration for teams that avoid handwritten JSON.

A representative production policy template separates deny, ask and trusted environment definitions:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Bash(git reset --hard *)",
      "Bash(terraform destroy *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(gh pr create *)"
    ]
  },
  "autoMode": {
    "environment": [
      "Source control: github.com/your-org and all repos under it",
      "Trusted internal domain: *.internal.example.com"
    ]
  }
}

Recommended usage segmentation

Workflows well suited for auto mode: local repository refactoring, test suite runs, installing pinned manifest dependencies, pushing personal feature branches.

Workflows that require mandatory human approval: production deployments, destructive git history changes, database migrations. These belong under permissions.ask.

Workflows that should not rely on auto‑mode classification alone: hosts holding production secrets, SSH keys or cloud credentials that process untrusted external input. These tasks require hardened containers, restricted network egress and dedicated sandboxes. Classifiers do not provide sufficient isolation against supply‑chain or module‑loading attacks.

API consumers running multi‑model agent stacks often manage permission policies and model routing centrally. 4sapi operates as an API gateway that unifies access across different model endpoints, letting teams standardize permission audit logging while switching between Claude, Codex and other compatible backends. This simplifies safety benchmarking when evaluating classifier behavior across model generations.

8. Final Risk Assessment and Practical Recommendations

Auto mode addresses a real operational pain point: permission fatigue. When users are forced to approve every trivial command, they stop inspecting prompts and click accept mechanically. A classifier that judges only the action, ignoring persuasive agent reasoning, can produce more consistent oversight than fatigued manual review. Still, auto mode improves default safety posture; it is not an infallible security boundary. Anthropic’s own 17% privilege‑escalation leakage rate, measured over a small corpus of 52 high‑risk cases, demonstrates the residual risk. The classifier evaluates single command syntax and lacks visibility into contextual state such as newly dropped files, modified modules or changing environment variables.

The practical operating guidance can be condensed into four points:

  1. Use auto mode for daily local development; it is safer than blanket --dangerously-skip-permissions.
  2. Route deployment, PR submission and destructive branch operations through permissions.ask to force human signoff.
  3. For untrusted inputs or credential‑bearing hosts, rely on sandboxes and network isolation rather than classifier judgment.
  4. Periodically validate active policy state with status checks to confirm whether auto mode enforcement is enabled.

The October rollout expands auto mode beyond developer terminals into mainstream Claude application sessions. More end users will interact with automated tool execution, which raises the importance of understanding its rule limits, classifier blind spots and measurable escape rates.

Domestic access: https://4sapi.org

medium.titulo: CLAUDE.md Nasıl Yazılır? Kötü ve İyi Örnek Yan Yana
medium.resumo: Aynı projeye yazılmış iki talimat dosyası, aynı soru ve Claude’un iki ayrı yolu
medium.conteudo_html:
Aynı projeye yazılmış iki talimat dosyası, aynı soru ve Claude’un iki ayrı yolu

Merhaba,

Bu yazımda sizlere Claude Code’un her oturumun başında okuduğu talimat dosyasını, CLAUDE.md’yi nasıl yazacağınızı anlatacağım. Aynı projeye yazılmış kötü ve iyi iki dosyayı yan yana koyacağım, sonra kendi dosyanızı yazıp sınamanın sırasını vereceğim.

Claude Code’la çalışırken testlerin hangi komutla koştuğunu, yeni dosyanın nereye konacağını, hangi modüle dikkatle dokunulacağını her oturumda yeniden anlatmak zorunda kalabilirsiniz. CLAUDE.md bu tekrarı bitirmek için var ama dosyanın var olması yetmiyor, içinde ne yazdığı belirleyici.

CLAUDE.md Nedir ve Neden Her Oturumda Okunur?

CLAUDE.md, projenizin kök dizininde duran sade bir markdown dosyasıdır. Claude her oturumun başında bu dosyayı okur.

Şöyle düşünün. Yeni işe başlayan bir geliştiriciye verdiğiniz ilk gün rehberi gibidir. Ekip neyi bilmesini istiyorsa rehbere yazar, yeni gelen kişi her seferinde sormak zorunda kalmaz.

İçine beş tür bilgi yazılır:

  • Komutlar: Derleme ve test komutlarının tam hali.
  • Kod stili: Girinti ve isimlendirme kuralları.
  • Mimari kararlar: Hangi dosya nerede durur, neden öyle kurgulanmış.
  • Konvansiyonlar: “Her zaman async/await kullan, callback değil” gibi proje alışkanlıkları.
  • Bilinen tuzaklar: Dokunmadan önce dikkat isteyen yerler.

Beşi de projenize yeni katılan birinin size soracağı soruların cevabıdır. Ekibinizde bir soru ne kadar çok sorulmuşsa, cevabını dosyaya yazmak o kadar işe yarar.

Dosya Nerede Durur, Kim Görür?

CLAUDE.md’nin durabileceği dört yer var, her birinin kapsamı başka.

  • ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md makinenizdeki her projeye uygulanır. Kişisel tercihleriniz burada durur, "yorumları hep Türkçe yaz" gibi.
  • Proje kökündeki ./CLAUDE.md git'e eklenir ve ekiple paylaşılır. Ekibin ortak kuralları burada yaşar.
  • ./CLAUDE.local.md projeye özel ama yalnız sizin makinenizde kalması gereken notlar içindir. .gitignore'a eklenir, ekip görmez.
  • .claude/rules/ klasöründeki kurallar yalnız ilgili dosya yollarına dokunulduğunda yüklenir.

CLAUDE.local.md dosyasını .gitignore'a eklemeyi unutmak sık yapılan bir hatadır. O zaman kişisel dosyanız bir commit'le ekibin ortak deposuna karışır. Dosyayı oluşturur oluşturmaz .gitignore kontrolünü yapmayı alışkanlık edinin.

Aynı Proje, İki Dosya

Kursta aynı projeyi iki klasöre koydum. Küçük bir sipariş servisi, iki klasörde de testleri yeşil. Tek fark CLAUDE.md dosyası.

Birinci klasördeki dosya yetmiş satır. Şöyle başlıyor:

# Proje Kuralları
Bu proje çok önemli bir projedir. Lütfen her zaman en iyi pratikleri uygula ve temiz kod
yaz. Kod kalitesine dikkat et. SOLID prensiplerine uy. Performansı her zaman göz önünde
bulundur ve optimize et. Kod kalitesi bizim için önceliklidir.
## Test
Test yazmak önemlidir. Testleri ihmal etme. Test kapsamı yeterli olsun. Testler
anlamlı olsun. Kırılgan testler yazma. Testleri çalıştırmayı unutma.

Dosyanın geri kalanı da böyle. Bölüm başlıkları var, kural yok. “İyi kod” kime göre iyi? Hangi komutla doğrulanacak? Hangi dosya nerede duruyor? Bu soruların cevabı yetmiş satırın hiçbirinde yok.

İkinci klasördeki dosyanın tamamı şu:

# siparis-servisi
Sipariş servisinin HTTP katmanı. Node.js, sıfır bağımlılık.
## Komutlar
- Test: `npm run test`
- Tek dosya: `node --test test/odeme.test.js`
## Konvansiyonlar
- Fonksiyon isimleri camelCase, dosya isimleri kebab-case
- API route'ları `src/api/` altında, her route kendi klasöründe (`src/api/<ad>/index.js`)
- Dışa açılan her modül `module.exports` ile tek nesne döndürür
## Tuzaklar
- `src/odeme/retry.js` içinde retry mantığı var; gecikme değerleri sağlayıcının rate
  limit eşiğine göre seçildi. Dokunmadan önce testleri mutlaka çalıştırın.
## İş bitti sayılma kuralı
Bir değişiklik, `npm run test` yeşil olmadan bitmiş sayılmaz. Test çıktısını göster.

Yirmi üç satırda bir test komutu, üç konvansiyon, bir tuzak ve işin ne zaman bitmiş sayılacağı var.

İyi bir CLAUDE.md uzun değil, somuttur. Uzunluk bir erdem değildir, çünkü her satır her oturumda bağlam penceresinden yer alır.

Aynı Soru, İki Yol

İki klasörde de Claude’a aynı soruyu sordum:

Testleri nasıl çalıştırıyoruz bu projede?

Kötü dosyanın durduğu klasörde Claude önce klasörü listeledi, sonra package.json dosyasını okudu, emin olmak için testleri çalıştırmayı denedi. Sonunda doğru cevabı buldu ama aramak zorunda kaldı, çünkü yetmiş satırlık dosya ona bu tek satırlık bilgiyi vermemişti.

İyi dosyanın durduğu klasörde cevap çok daha çabuk geldi: npm run test. Tek bir doğrulama adımı yetti. Claude aramadı, zaten bildiğini teyit etti.

Bir soruda kazanılan birkaç saniye önemsiz görünebilir. Gün içinde onlarca soru sorduğunuzda bu saniyeler birikir, okunan her gereksiz dosya da bağlamdan yer alır.

Dosyanın etkisi sorularla sınırlı değil. İyi dosyanın durduğu klasörde bir de iş istedim:

Kullanıcı profilini güncelleyen yeni bir API route ekle.

Claude yeni dosyayı doğrudan src/api/profil/index.js yoluna koydu, nereye koyacağını bana sormadı. İşi bitirirken testleri de çalıştırıp çıktısını gösterdi. İkisini de ben söylemedim, dosyada yazıyordu. İlk soruda Claude bilgiye erişti, burada kurala uydu.

İyi Bir CLAUDE.md’nin İlkeleri

  • Kısa tutun. İki yüz satırı geçmeyin. Her satır her oturumda yüklenir.
  • Somut yazın. “İyi kod” değil, “şu komutla test et”.
  • Örnekle anlatın. Soyut kural yerine gerçek bir kod parçacığı daha etkilidir.
  • Güncel tutun. Proje değiştikçe dosya da değişir.
  • Nadir gereken bilgiyi skill’e taşıyın. Uzun bir stil kılavuzu ya da API dokümantasyonu her oturumda yüklenmesin.

CLAUDE.md bir istek listesi değil, bir kısıtlama listesidir. “Temiz kod yaz” derseniz on geliştiriciden on farklı cevap alırsınız. “Fonksiyon isimleri camelCase olmalı” derseniz tek bir doğru cevap vardır ve Claude’a yorum payı kalmaz.

Dosyanın neden kısa kalması gerektiğini, yani bağlam penceresinin nasıl dolduğunu context window yazısında ayrıca anlatıyorum.

Kendi Dosyanızı Yazın ve Sınayın

Sıfırdan yazmayın. Proje klasörünüzde bir oturum açıp /init komutunu çalıştırın. Claude kod tabanını tarar ve bir taslak çıkarır. Projenizde zaten bir CLAUDE.md varsa /init üzerine yazmaz, iyileştirme önerir.

Taslak ham haliyle kusurludur. Onu dört soruyla süzün:

  • Kısa mı? İki yüz satırı geçiyorsa budayın.
  • Somut mu? Genel geçer cümleleri silin ya da somut bir kurala çevirin.
  • Doğru mu? Claude’un tahmin ettiği komut, gerçekte kullandığınızdan farklıysa düzeltin.
  • Eksik mi? Sizin bildiğiniz ama Claude’un dosyalardan çıkaramayacağı kuralı ekleyin.

Dördüncü soru en değerlisi. Tuzaklar koddan değil geçmişten gelir, /init onları bilemez. "Bu modüle elle dokunmayın, otomatik üretiliyor" gibi bir satırı ancak siz yazabilirsiniz.

Sonra sınayın. /clear ile bağlamı sıfırlayın ki cevap konuşma geçmişinden değil dosyadan gelsin. Ardından kuralınıza dokunan bir soru sorun. Claude dosyaları taramadan, tahmin etmeden kuralı söylüyorsa dosya çalışıyor demektir. Hâlâ tahmin ediyorsa kural yeterince net değildir, yeniden yazın.

Soruyu iyi seçin. Cevabı koda bakarak bulunabilen bir soru farkı göstermez. Cevabı yalnız sizin bildiğiniz bir soru gösterir:

Bu projeye jest kurup testleri onunla yazabilir miyim?

Bir de uyarı: /clear kalıcı hafızayı silmez. Oturum sırasında Claude'a "bunu hatırla" dediyseniz not CLAUDE.md'ye değil, Claude'un kendi hafıza klasörüne yazılır ve /clear sonrası da yüklenir. Aldığınız doğru cevap dosyanızdan değil o nottan geliyor olabilir. Emin olmak için /memory ile hafıza klasörüne bakın.

Sık Yapılan Hatalar

  • Dilek listesi yazmak. “Kaliteli kod istiyorum”, “performanslı olsun” niyet bildirir, talimat vermez. Kaliteyi nasıl ölçeceğinizi yazın.
  • Dosyayı bir kez yazıp bir daha açmamak. Mimari değişince eski kural yanlış hale gelir ve Claude o yanlış kurala sadık kalmaya çalışır.
  • Kişisel notu ortak dosyaya koymak. Yalnız sizin makinenizle ilgili bilgi ekip arkadaşlarınız için anlamsız ya da yanıltıcıdır.
  • Sınamadan “bitti” demek. Yazdığınız her kuralı en az bir soruyla deneyin.

Kötü bir CLAUDE.md, boş bir CLAUDE.md’den de kötüdür, çünkü yanlış bilgi Claude’u yanlış yönlendirir. CLAUDE.md ayrıca bir ricadır. Dosyayı sistem uygulamaz, Claude yorumlar. Bozulduğunda geri alamayacağınız bir kuralı ricaya bırakmayın. O tür kuralların nasıl zorlandığını hook’ları anlattığım yazıda ele alıyorum.

Toparlarsak

CLAUDE.md yazmak kolaydır, doğrulamak zordur. Kısa ve somut yazın, sonra temiz bir konuşmada tek bir soruyla sınayın. Claude’un davranışı değişmediyse dosya henüz bitmemiştir.

İki klasörün yan yana ekran karşılaştırmasını ve kendi projeniz için dosya yazdığınız lab’ı adım adım görmek isteyenler için Udemy’de bir eğitim hazırladım. İlgilenirseniz diye bırakıyorum: Claude Code: Yapay Zeka Ajanıyla Kodlama ve İş Otomasyonu.

medium.titulo: Can Your IDE Catch Accessibility Issues Before QA?
medium.resumo: Bringing accessibility feedback closer to the code, without replacing human judgment.
medium.conteudo_html:
Bringing accessibility feedback closer to the code, without replacing human judgment.

Accessibility Shouldn’t Have to Wait for a Test Cycle

Picture a familiar scenario.

A developer finishes a feature, opens a pull request, and everything looks ready. The interface works, the API integration is complete, and the component behaves exactly as expected during mouse-based testing.

A few days later, QA identifies several accessibility issues.

A button cannot be reached using the keyboard. An icon-only control has no accessible name. A custom dropdown looks polished but does not communicate its expanded state to assistive technologies.

None of these problems necessarily requires a major architectural change. Yet fixing them late means reopening work, reviewing the implementation, repeating tests, and potentially delaying delivery.

What if developers received meaningful accessibility feedback while writing the component?

This is the question I have been exploring: Can we move accessibility feedback directly into the development environment, before a pull request even exists?

The Gap Between Writing Code and Validating Accessibility

Modern development environments are remarkably good at identifying problems early.

TypeScript catches type mismatches. ESLint flags suspicious patterns. Formatters enforce consistency. Framework tooling helps identify invalid usage and potential runtime issues.

Accessibility, however, is often treated differently.

Developers may rely on browser extensions, automated audits, QA processes, or accessibility specialists to identify issues after the interface has already been implemented.

These tools are valuable, but the feedback frequently arrives outside the moment when the developer is making the relevant decision.

Consider a simple Vue component:

<template>
  <div class="search-button" @click="openSearch">
    <SearchIcon />
  </div>
</template>

Visually, it might work perfectly.

From an accessibility perspective, though, it raises several questions:

  • Is the control keyboard accessible?
  • Does it expose the correct semantics?
  • Does it have an accessible name?
  • Can assistive technologies identify its purpose?

The better implementation is often straightforward:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="search-button"
    aria-label="Open search"
    @click="openSearch"
  >
    <SearchIcon aria-hidden="true" />
  </button>
</template>

The important difference is not the number of lines.

It is the engineering decision to use a native interactive element rather than recreate its behavior unnecessarily.

An IDE-based accessibility check could help surface that decision immediately.

What Static Analysis Can Actually Detect

Not every accessibility problem can be identified by inspecting source code.

However, many common patterns can be detected or flagged for review.

In Vue projects, useful checks might include:

1. Images without meaningful alternatives

<img :src="product.image" />

A tool can identify the missing alt attribute. It cannot automatically determine whether the image is informative or decorative.

2. Click handlers on non-interactive elements

<div @click="submitForm">
  Submit
</div>

This pattern deserves attention because keyboard interaction and semantic behavior may be missing.

3. Form controls without associated labels

<input v-model="email" type="email" />

An editor can flag the absence of an obvious accessible naming mechanism, while recognizing that some labels may be provided through component abstractions.

4. ARIA attributes with invalid values

<button aria-expanded="maybe">
  Options
</button>

Some ARIA attributes have explicitly defined allowed values. These are good candidates for deterministic validation.

5. Custom interactive components

Components that implement dialogs, menus, tabs, or comboboxes may require additional review of focus management, keyboard interaction, and state communication.

These examples suggest a useful distinction:

Static analysis can identify patterns and risks. It cannot establish that an entire user experience is accessible.

That limitation should shape how the tooling is designed.

Why Vue Makes This Interesting

Vue’s component architecture creates opportunities for accessibility checks, but also introduces challenges.

A component may receive its accessible name through a prop. Its underlying semantic element may be rendered dynamically. A reusable design-system component may encapsulate keyboard handling internally.

For example:

<BaseButton
  variant="primary"
  icon="search"
  label="Open search"
  @click="openSearch"
/>

Without understanding how BaseButton works, a simple analyzer might incorrectly flag this component.

The presence of a label prop does not automatically guarantee an accessible name, either. That depends on how the component renders it.

This is where developer tooling needs to become more context-aware.

A practical approach could combine:

  • Vue template parsing.
  • Rules for native HTML elements.
  • Knowledge of registered design-system components.
  • Configurable mappings for accessibility-related props.
  • Clear explanations of potential issues.
  • Suggestions that prioritize semantic HTML.

The objective should not be to generate as many warnings as possible.

It should be to deliver feedback developers can trust.

Where AI Can Help, and Where It Shouldn’t Decide

AI-assisted development adds another dimension.

Traditional static analysis works particularly well when rules are explicit and deterministic.

For example, checking whether aria-expanded contains a valid value does not require a language model.

But other questions are more contextual.

Does an image’s alternative text describe its purpose? Is a control’s accessible name meaningful? Does a proposed interaction pattern make sense for the user’s task?

AI may help developers investigate these questions by explaining context, proposing improvements, or highlighting potential concerns.

Still, an AI-generated recommendation is not equivalent to verified accessibility.

A useful model would separate three kinds of feedback:

Deterministic findings: Problems supported by explicit rules or reliably detectable patterns.

Contextual warnings: Potential issues requiring a developer to inspect surrounding behavior.

AI-assisted suggestions: Recommendations that may improve an implementation but require human validation.

This separation matters because confidence should be earned, not implied.

A developer should know whether a warning represents a confirmed rule violation or a hypothesis worth investigating.

Designing Feedback That Developers Will Actually Use

Developer experience is central to the effectiveness of any accessibility tool.

If an extension produces hundreds of noisy warnings, developers will eventually ignore them.

If it interrupts every keystroke, it becomes frustrating.

If it proposes unnecessary ARIA attributes, it may even encourage worse implementations.

A more useful experience would follow a few principles.

Explain the problem, not just the rule

Instead of displaying:

Accessibility violation: non-interactive element.

Explain:

This element handles a click event but may not support keyboard activation. Consider using a native button if the element performs an action.

Offer a practical next step

Warnings should help developers understand how to improve the code without automatically rewriting complex interactions.

Support progressive feedback

Lightweight checks can run while editing. More expensive analysis can run when saving a file, reviewing a component, or preparing a pull request.

Respect existing design systems

Organizations often have established component libraries. Tooling should understand those abstractions instead of treating every custom component as inherently inaccessible.

Avoid turning accessibility into a score

A single percentage can create a misleading impression of completeness.

Passing automated checks does not mean that keyboard navigation, screen reader interaction, cognitive accessibility, or the overall user experience has been adequately validated.

Exploring an Accessibility-First Developer Workflow

These ideas have led me toward an experimental direction I am calling AccessLens.

The concept is a developer-focused accessibility assistant that could integrate with environments such as VS Code and Cursor, initially concentrating on Vue components.

The goal would be to identify selected accessibility risks close to the source code and provide actionable, contextual feedback.

An initial exploration could focus on a small number of rules:

  • Native interactive semantics.
  • Accessible naming.
  • Image alternatives.
  • Selected ARIA validation.
  • Common keyboard accessibility risks.

More advanced capabilities, including design-system awareness and AI-assisted explanations, could be explored incrementally.

This is a research and prototyping direction, not a claim that a finished tool already exists.

The engineering challenge is not simply detecting patterns. It is determining which findings are reliable, which require context, and how to communicate that distinction clearly.

I am particularly interested in evaluating false positives, the usefulness of suggested fixes, and how early feedback changes the developer workflow.

Accessibility Is Still a Human Responsibility

Even with better tooling, accessibility cannot be reduced to automated validation.

A component may pass static checks and still be confusing to use.

A dialog may expose the correct roles while handling focus incorrectly.

A form may have labels but present error messages that are difficult to understand.

Meaningful accessibility evaluation still requires interaction testing, keyboard navigation, assistive technologies, and human judgment.

The purpose of earlier feedback is not to eliminate those practices.

It is to help developers address preventable issues sooner, so later testing can focus on more complex questions about real usability.

The Next Step Is Closer to the Code

In my previous articles, I explored why accessibility should become part of the development workflow and how Vue components can be designed with accessibility in mind.

The next question is how to make those principles easier to apply consistently.

For me, that means looking beyond another checklist or final-stage audit.

It means exploring tools that can recognize common risks, explain why they matter, and help developers make better decisions while the implementation is still taking shape.

The earlier we make accessibility visible, the more naturally it becomes part of engineering quality.

And perhaps the most useful accessibility warning is the one a developer receives before the problem ever reaches QA.

I’m a Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead working across enterprise software, digital commerce, and accessible web experiences. I write about practical engineering approaches that help teams build more reliable, inclusive, and maintainable products.

medium.titulo: Wikinewsie (open-source bug) — Fix untranslated labels after switching languages
medium.resumo: In this article, I would like to write about a bug in Wikinewsie and how I tackled it.
medium.conteudo_html:
In this article, I would like to write about a bug in Wikinewsie and how I tackled it.

Here are a few quick things to know.

Wikinewsie is a web app that shows the most-edited Wikipedia.org articles over recent hours, automatically identifying current event topics and news that are undergoing active collaboration.

Wikimedia keeps its bug list on a website called Phabricator. Every bug gets a number starting with the letter T. Ours is T439940.

Here is the Open-source loop: Find a bug, make a branch, change the code, test it, save it, send it for review.

Fix untranslated labels in Wikinewsie after switching language: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough

The Bug Report:

Steps to replicate the issue (include links if applicable):

Open https://wikinewsie.toolforge.org/en
Use the language selector to pick another language (e.g., Polish)
What happens?:
Most of the elements are translated, but several are not.
In the Feed section -
*"Mix"
*"Editors"
*"Edits"

In the Mix weights section -

*"Edits"
*"Editors"
*"Growth"
*"Category"
*"New page"

What should have happened instead?:

These elements should have been shown in the newly selected language, instead of retaining the language of the initial selection.
Note that the bug doesn't appear when Polish interface is loaded directly, only when English is loaded first and then the language selector is used to switch to Polish.
Software version (on Special:Version page; skip for WMF-hosted wikis like Wikipedia):

Explaination:
On the Wikinewsie site, when someone opens the English version first and then uses the language dropdown to switch to Polish, most of the page changes to Polish, but a few words stay in English. Those words are:

  • In the Feed section: “Mix”, “Editors”, “Edits”
  • In the Mix weights section: “Edits”, “Editors”, “Growth”, “Category”, “New page”

Why does the bug matter? Think of a Polish reader. They pick Polish from the language dropdown and expect everything on the page in Polish. If a few buttons still say “Mix”, “Editors” and “Edits” in English, the page feels half-finished and confusing.

The plan

1. Make a new branch, so our work stays separate from the main code.
2. Find where the translations are stored.
3. Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.
4. Find where the code uses those keys.
5. Work out why they do not update.
6. Fix it
7. Test it
8. Check that we changed only what we meant to change.
9. Commit, push, and open a merge request.

Switch to a new branch

git checkout -b fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

Find where the translations are stored

Why we need it? Before fixing anything, we need to know where the words come from. We searched the whole project for one of the stuck labels.

grep -rni "mix weights" i18n src

What did we get?

./i18n/en.json:90:      "wikinewsie-mix-weights-label": "Mix weights:",

We learned two things from this:

1. The `i18n` folder holds the translations. (“i18n” is short for “internationalization”, which just means “making the app work in many languages”).

2. Think of it like a dictionary. The code asks for the key wikinewsie-mix-weights-label, and the language file hands back the right words Mix weights.

Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.

We open the file i18/en.json and copy all the keys for the missing labels.

"wikinewsie-mix": "Mix",
"wikinewsie-edits": "Edits",
"wikinewsie-editors": "Editors",
"wikinewsie-growth": "Growth",
"wikinewsie-category": "Category",
"wikinewsie-new-page": "New page",

All six keys exist in the translation files. This confirms what the report hinted at: the translations are fine, so the problem must be in how the code uses them.

Find where the code uses these keys

We searched the `src` folder (where the app’s code lives) for the “Mix” key.

grep -rn "wikinewsie-mix'" src

The quote after the key makes it match wikinewsie-mix exactly, and not longer keys such as wikinewsie-mix-score

We found the culprit in src/App.vue :

const MODE_OPTIONS: Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }> = [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
];

Here is what each piece in that code is.

  • text('wikinewsie-mix') is the function that looks up a key and returns the words in the current language.
  • MODE_OPTIONS is the list of buttons for the Feed section.

Now the important part: when does text(…)run?

It runs once, at the moment the file loads and the list is created. At that moment the language is English, so the label is locked in as the plain word “Mix”. Later, when the user switches to Polish, the language changes, but this list is already built. Nobody rebuilds it. It keeps saying “Mix”.

It is like printing a menu. If you print it in English and the customer later asks for Polish, the printed menu does not change by itself. You have to print a new one.

Solution
Vue (the framework this app uses) has something called `computed` because of this Vue re-runs the whenever something it depends on changes.

We make the change to MODE_OPTIONS by adding computed

const MODE_OPTIONS = computed<Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }>>(() => [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
]);

What changed:

  • The list is wrapped in computed(() => [...])

So far, we have got MODE_OPTIONS labels (Mix, Editors, Edits) covered now.

We go on to the next labels for WEIGHTS(Edits, Editors, Growth, Category, New page)

We begin by searching for the keys that only this list uses

grep -n "wikinewsie-growth\|wikinewsie-category\|wikinewsie-new-page" src/App.vue

That led us to WEIGHTS_FIELDS. We checked where it is used and just as the previous one, we have to add computed

BEFORE:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS: Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }> = [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
];

AFTER:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS = computed<Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }>>(() => [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
]);
  • The list is now wrapped in computed(() => [...])

We saved the file, switched English to Polish in the running app, and both the Feed buttons and Weights buttons changed immediately to Polish.

Save the changes and Push

git add src/App.vue
git commit -m "Fix untranslated labels after switching language"
git push -u origin fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

corrida_no_ar.titulo: CAMPEÃ OLÍMPICA Peres Jepchirchir PEGA NO DOPING
corrida_no_ar.resumo: O mundo da maratona é abalado com a notícia do doping da campeã olímpica Peres Jepchirchir. Conheça também o calendário 2027 do Mountain Do, o novo e surreal Puma Fast-R 2, e saiba quem é o novo embaixador de peso da Coros.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sábado | 24 de outubro de 2026

Uma notícia chocante abalou o mundo da maratona: Peres Jepchirchir, uma das atletas de elite mais importantes da história, foi pega no exame antidoping. A queniana, campeã olímpica em Tóquio, campeã mundial de maratona e atual recordista mundial da meia maratona em provas exclusivamente femininas, teve um resultado adverso para EPO. O teste foi realizado fora de competição, no Quênia, antes de ela vencer a Maratona de Sydney, onde bateu o recorde da prova. Jepchirchir, que já venceu as Maratonas de Londres, Nova York, Boston e Valência, está suspensa provisoriamente. A notícia foi divulgada pelo perfil da Maratona de Sydney, já que o site da Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) está em manutenção. Pelas regras das World Marathon Majors, qualquer atleta suspenso por doping por três meses ou mais é banido para sempre de todas as oito provas do circuito. Este caso se soma a uma longa lista de mais de 140 atletas quenianos suspensos nos últimos cinco anos.

Mountain Do divulga calendário para 2027

Para quem gosta de uma boa aventura, o Mountain Do anunciou seu calendário para 2027, com 10 etapas em 5 países. O circuito, conhecido por suas provas em locais deslumbrantes e kits completos, passará por diversos territórios, incluindo floresta, deserto, montanha e cerrado. As etapas confirmadas são: Colônia do Sacramento (Uruguai) em 14 de março; Praia do Rosa (SC) em 3 de abril; Deserto da Namíbia em 5 de junho; Chapada dos Veadeiros (GO) em 27 de junho; Costão do Santinho (SC) em 10 de julho; Fim do Mundo em Ushuaia (Argentina) em 7 de agosto; Fernando de Noronha (PE) em 11 de setembro; Selva Amazônica em Macapá (AP) em 26 de setembro; Deserto do Saara (Marrocos) em 7 de novembro; e Pantanal (MS) em 27 de novembro. Fique atento, pois em breve o canal deve divulgar um cupom de desconto.

Puma lança o “pula-pula” Fast-R 2

A Puma anunciou o seu novo supertênis, o Fast-R 2, um modelo com design surrealista e exagerado. Apelidado de “pula-pula”, o tênis se deforma visivelmente a cada pisada, funcionando como uma espécie de trampolim. O modelo é totalmente proibido para uso pela elite em competições oficiais, mas promete uma experiência de corrida única para amadores. O lançamento está previsto para o dia 28 de outubro.

John Korir é o novo embaixador da Coros

O atleta queniano John Korir, tricampeão de World Marathon Majors com vitórias em Chicago e Boston, é o novo embaixador da Coros. Com um sorriso contagiante, Korir se junta à marca de relógios esportivos, que agora tem um atleta de altíssimo nível para preencher o espaço deixado pela equipe de Eliud Kipchoge, que mudou de patrocinador. Atualmente, John Korir está treinando para a Maratona de Valência com o objetivo de correr a distância abaixo de 2 horas.
